LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Say Hello, Make Space, Be Curious & Ask Nicely — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson is the joining-in kit: four words that open doors, save seats, start friendships and get things gently — rehearsed at home so the playground feels already played.

What is this?

Say hello opens the door, make space saves the seat, be curious asks about the other person, and ask nicely gets things without grabbing — the four smallest words with the biggest social mileage.

What does it mean?

Most friendships at four start with logistics, not chemistry: someone said hello, someone scooted over, someone asked a question. Children who own the logistics get more at-bats — and friendships are a numbers game at first.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: hello comes in all sizes (wave, smile, whisper — all count); making space is a BODY move (scoot, slide, make room) that says you belong here without a word; and be curious flips the spotlight — the fastest way to be interesting is to be interested.

Why this matters

This card turns the class’s inner words outward at playground scale: the feeling words become door-words. It sits right before the cooperation card because joining is step one; building together is step two.

What it teaches

Social initiation (the hello), spatial inclusion (making room), conversational curiosity (asking about others), and polite requesting — the may-I that replaces the grab everywhere it is installed.

Words to learn

say hellomake spacebe curiousask nicelyjoin inmay Iscoot

Say this to your child

“"Here is how you get into any game, anywhere. One: say hello — big wave, small smile, even a whisper; a hello is a hello, and it opens the door. Two: make space — scoot over, slide along, hold the blanket open; making room says you belong here louder than words. Three: be curious — ask the new friend something: what do you like? what can that truck do? Being interested in someone is the fastest way to become their friend. Four: ask nicely — may I have a turn, please? Works on toys, swings, crayons and almost every grown-up alive. Four small words. Whole friendships start with less."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four words that get you into the game."
  2. Read the panels: the waving boy SAYs HELLO, the hand-on-chest girl MAKEs SPACE, the wondering boy BEs CURIOUS, the folded-hands girl ASKs NICELY.
  3. Rehearse on toys (below) before people — two stuffed animals run the whole sequence: hello, scoot, "what do you like?", "may I borrow the crayon?"
  4. Practise three hellos in the mirror: big wave, quiet smile, silly eyebrow — all valid.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "the game does not start until someone says hello — be the someone."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the joining-in words: Say Hello, a waving boy; Make Space, a girl with a hand on her chest stepping aside; Be Curious, a boy wondering with a finger to his chin; and Ask Nicely, a girl asking with hands folded together — the kit drawn at playground-door size.

Ask your child

"What are the three sizes of hello?" "What does make space look like on a bench?" "What question could you ask a new friend?" "What works better than grabbing?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Hello — want to play?" (the whole door, three words) "here is space for you!" or the report: "I asked nicely and she said YES."

Out in the real world

Doors open all week: the new child at story time, the cousin arriving, the shared sandbox, the school open day. Run the kit in miniature on the way in — "shall we say hello first, or make space first?" — and let your child pick the door they open.

Try it together

The Toy Playdate: two stuffed animals meet at a tiny bench. Your child runs both roles (or you take one): hello (different voices are encouraged), make space on the bench, be curious — "what do YOU like?" — and ask nicely for the shared crayon. Swap roles, run it again, then retire the toys and deploy the same four moves at the real playground this week.

Understanding check

Ask: "What opens the door? What does make space say without words? What works better than grabbing?" Hello, you belong here, asking nicely — three answers and the joining-in kit is packed.

Parent tips

Resist scripting the friendship — hand over the four moves and let your child’s version be weird if it wants; a robot-dance hello that lands is worth more than a polished one that never leaves the house. And when the ask-nicely fails (it will sometimes), debrief the Ask, not the rejection: "good asking. Sometimes the answer is not yet — want to try again after her turn?"

This lesson pairs with the Say Hello, Make Space, Be Curious & Ask Nicely flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
